narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 66.3% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is well above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. By far the strongest influence was your third-year class ranking. Placing in the bottom decile of your class was a significant red flag that strongly pushed the prediction toward failure. Your first-year ranking in the middle of the pack (decile 5 out of 10) worked in the opposite direction and helped the model somewhat, but its positive effect was much smaller than the negative impact from your third year. Your LSAT score of 34 also pulled the prediction slightly toward failure; while not dramatically low, it sits below the average of students who were admitted.

Taken together, these academic signals led the model to conclude that the risk of bar exam failure was too high to approve your admission.

What you should do next is focus on strengthening the areas the model weighed most heavily. Retaking the LSAT to raise your score, improving your study habits to move up in class rank if you are still in school, or gaining additional legal experience that demonstrates your ability to succeed could all help improve your profile for future applications.
